When a primary school replaced its evening homework with twenty minutes of reading, the staff expected complaints from parents, and the head had cleared an hour of her week for meetings. (1) ______

The reasoning was simple. Homework set for a class of thirty is either too easy for some children or too hard for others, and the child who most needs the practice is the least likely to do it at home; nor does a worksheet tell a teacher which of the thirty has understood the rule and which has copied from a neighbour. (2) ______

Reading was chosen for a practical reason: it can be done at any level, and a child who is behind can read the same book as a child who is ahead without either of them noticing: a child who finishes a book in a week is not held back, and a child who takes a month is not exposed as slow. (3) ______ A teacher who once set thirty identical worksheets now spends the same hour reading aloud, and reports that she knows her class better than she did before; the library, which used to open twice a week, now opens every morning before lessons.

The results after two years are modest and hard to dispute. Children read more books, and the gap between the fastest and slowest readers narrowed slightly, and the staff report that children now talk about books at break, which no worksheet had ever made them do. (4) ______ Both changes remain small enough that a sceptical parent could reasonably describe them as a coincidence.

Not everyone is satisfied. Some parents complain that without worksheets they cannot see what their child is doing, and that a child who reads quietly may be reading nothing at all. (5) ______ The school now sends home a single line each week describing what the child read, which the head admits is a compromise rather than a solution. Whether that is enough is a question the school expects to be asked again next term.

When a small museum in the north replaced its professional audio guide with recordings made by visitors, the staff expected complaints from the trustees. (1) ______

The old guide had been thorough. It described every object in ninety seconds of measured prose, in two languages, read by an actor, and it had been praised in a national newspaper for the clarity of its writing. It was also, according to the museum's own data, listened to by fewer than a fifth of visitors, and switched off most often at the third object.

The new recordings are uneven in every way. A retired teacher talks about a bowl for four minutes and never mentions its date; a boy of nine explains a model engine with far more enthusiasm than accuracy; a farmer describes a tool that his own grandfather used, and cries halfway through. (2) ______

What the staff had not anticipated was how the recordings would change the way people moved through the rooms. Visitors who took the visitor-made guide spent, on average, eleven minutes longer in the building, and they were far more likely to stop and speak to one another at the cases. (3) ______ The benches by the door, installed for the elderly, were occupied all afternoon by people of twenty.

There is an argument against all of this, and the curator makes it herself. A museum's authority rests on the claim that somebody knows which account is accurate, and a guide made by visitors cannot make that claim at all. (4) ______ She has therefore added a single recorded sentence before each visitor's contribution, naming the object and stating what is known about it, and she has kept the old guide available on a second channel for those who want it.

The first year's figures are not decisive either way. Use of the guide rose from eighteen per cent of visitors to sixty, and donations rose slightly, though the museum cannot say whether the two are connected. (5) ______ What she says she has learned is narrower and more useful: people listen to a voice that sounds like their own, and a museum that speaks only in its own voice is addressing a smaller room than it believes.

Her solution was not to abandon the experiment but to frame it.
The building, in other words, had become a place to talk in rather than a place to look at.
Neither figure explains why the rooms feel different, and the curator does not pretend that they do.
For example, a museum in the south has removed its guide altogether.
In short, professional guides should be abolished in every museum.

For forty years the river ran under four lanes of concrete, and the only sign of it was the name of the road. The road had been built in 1971, on a plan that assumed the river could be moved somewhere else. When the motorway was demolished in 2011, the water reappeared within a month, brown and slow, in a channel that nobody had cleaned.

The plan had been to build offices on the land, and the drawings had already been approved. (1) ______

The reason for the second thoughts was a flood. Two winters of heavy rain showed that the concrete had been doing work nobody had credited it with: it carried water away fast, and the streets it protected were now the streets that flooded. (2) ______

The river was reopened in stages, and each stage was cheaper than the engineers had feared. A channel was dug, the banks were planted, and the rest was left to the water, which within three years had made bends that no designer would have drawn. (3) ______ The photographs on the council's website make it look as though the park had always been there, and the council has decided not to correct that impression.

What the city has gained is not only drainage. Property beside the water is now worth more than the offices would have been, and the path along the bank carries, on a Sunday, more people than the motorway ever did. (4) ______ The benches are the most used piece of public furniture the city owns, according to the annual survey.

There are costs, and the city does not hide them. Two car parks were lost, the bus route had to be redrawn, and the shops on the old road lost the passing trade they had depended on for decades, and two of those shops have since closed without compensation. (5) ______ The council now says it would do the same again, and says so in a report that lists every objection it received.

Those losses are real, and they fell on people with the least room to absorb them.

A factory that makes parts for lifts has let its two hundred workers choose their own shifts since 2016, when the personnel manager found that no wage could fill the Friday night shift.

The system is simple and has one rule: every shift must be covered. (1) ______ Anyone who wants a particular shift must find a colleague to work it with them, and the pair then register the swap on a screen by the door.

What the manager did not expect was that the choice would sort itself by age and by school hours rather than by pay. Parents of young children took the early shift, the youngest workers took nights, and the weekend shifts, which had been the hardest to fill, are now the easiest, because they suit people who want four consecutive days away from the plant. (2) ______

The figures are better than the manager's own forecast. Absence has fallen by a fifth, output per hour has risen slightly, and the factory has not used an agency worker in three years, which saves more than the software costs. (3) ______

There are costs that the figures do not show. Two workers who had chosen nights for years discovered that nobody wanted to cover their holidays, and the manager had to write a rule that was not in the plan: a chosen shift is a promise, and a promise has to be negotiated rather than announced. (4) ______ The people who gained most from the freedom, it turned out, were the ones with the least bargaining power, because a worker with options is a worker who can ask.

What the manager will not say is that the system would work everywhere. It works here because the work is predictable and the workforce is stable, and a factory with a seasonal order book would find the promise much harder to keep. (5) ______ He says he would rather be asked about the two hundred than about the ten thousand, and that the question he is asked most often is why he did not try it sooner.

passages.passage:
In many families, practical knowledge passes silently from one generation to the next, yet it is often lost when young people move to cities, live alone, or depend on professional services for every small problem. An older relative may know how to make a knife sharp, repair damaged clothing, or judge when bread has grown, but such skills often remain unnoticed until the person who holds them is no longer nearby. When the older person stops being able to demonstrate a task, the gap may feel like a sudden loss rather than a gradual absence of memory. Digital videos offer useful access to information, and they can show a procedure from several angles, but information alone does not create judgment. (1) ______

A family kitchen or work area can become a place for teaching when adults explain not only what to do but also how to notice when something is going wrong. A young person who cooks with an aunt learns to listen for the change in sound as water begins to boil and to feel when dough has been pressed enough, and those signals are difficult to describe without practice. (2) ______

The process also changes the relationship between generations. Young people are often seen as learners, while older relatives are seen as providers of advice; when they complete a practical task together, both roles become more equal and more flexible. (3) ______

Specific traditions matter as well because they carry memory and identity, not just technique. (4) ______ Teaching can fail when it becomes a test or a performance, so the atmosphere should leave room for mistakes, questions, and repeated attempts. A family that laughs at a badly shaped dumpling is more likely to continue the lesson than one that treats every error as evidence of carelessness. (5) ______

The goal is not to preserve every old method exactly as it was once used. It is to give young people enough practical confidence to solve problems, appreciate the knowledge around them, and pass something useful forward when their own turn comes.
